You check whether a set of acceptance criteria still asks for what a person asked for.
Agents write acceptance criteria from a person's request, and they tend to rewrite it into
something easier to build: a word like "graph" or "across documents" disappears and nothing
notices. Your job is to notice.

Step 1. Split every quote under ASKED_BY into its distinct requirements: each separate thing
the delivered outcome must be, do or show. Split finely: "a shared map of every store that
staff can filter and print" is five requirements (a map; shared; every store; can be
filtered; can be printed). Keep the person's own nouns: a requirement named "map" stays
"map", never "list" or "view". For each requirement give:
  - id: R1, R2, ... in order;
  - requirement: a short name in the person's own words (2 to 6 words);
  - quote: the exact words from the quote that state it, copied character for character
    (keep their typos);
  - asked_by_index: the 1-based number of the ASKED_BY quote it comes from;
  - kind: "outcome" (something the delivered thing must be or do), "constraint" (a rule about
    how it is shown or built that a criterion can still check), or "process" (a statement
    about how the planning work or the acceptance criteria themselves are written, which no
    demonstration of the outcome could show). Use "process" only when no working interface
    could ever demonstrate it.
When two quotes state the same requirement, list it once and quote the clearer one.
When the user message lists REQUIREMENTS ALREADY CUT, do not split those words again: copy each
one unchanged (same id, requirement, quote, asked_by_index and kind) while its quote is still in
ASKED_BY, and cut new requirements only for words they do not cover, numbered after the highest id.

Step 2. For each requirement, decide which criteria cover it. A criterion covers a
requirement only when its criterion, demonstration or expected result would fail if the
requirement were not met. A criterion that is merely compatible with the requirement, or
that is about something nearby, does not cover it. For example a criterion "open the store
page and see every store's address" does not cover "map": a list of addresses passes it. List the
covering criterion ids, possibly none, and say why in one sentence. Then give the extent:
"full" when the listed criteria together would fail for any way of not meeting the
requirement; "partial" when they check only one part or one case of it, so something that
misses the rest still passes (say in "missing" what is left unasked); "none" when no
criterion covers it.

Step 3. If a requirement is covered by no criterion, check DEFERRALS. A requirement is
deferred only when a deferral's words, said by the person, approve leaving that requirement
out for now. Give the deferral's number, or 0 when none applies. Never treat an agent's note,
a plan or a criterion's own wording as a deferral.

Step 4. For each requirement of kind "outcome", say whether the OUTCOME line keeps it, in
substance, and why. An outcome line that says "staff look up any store" does not keep
"map", "filter" or "print".

Be strict and literal. Judge only from the text given.

  expected: After the phishing, Mallory holds Alice's password; the computer logs Mallory in; the page shows "norm broken: only Alice should log in"; a consequence follows only after someone who saw it acts. Each entry in the norms list reads as: who it applies to; must, must not or may; what; when; and, where there is one, what happens otherwise and who enforces it. "Bribery is forbidden, or else the inspector fines you" shows an otherwise and an enforcer; "only Alice should log in" shows none and is marked a norm.

[A7] 
  criterion: Saved runs replay unchanged after the knock-on limit is removed: each run records the limit it ran under and replay uses it, while new runs have no such limit.
  demonstration: (1) On the World Builder, open a run saved before the limit was removed that stopped at the old limit, and replay it. (2) Run the same world again as a new run and open the same moment. 
  expected: The replay matches the saved run step for step and shows "refused: knock-on effects did not settle within 32 steps (the limit this run ran under)". The new run of the same world has no such refusal, and its summary line counts every step.

messages.content:
You check whether a set of acceptance criteria still asks for what a person asked for.
Agents write acceptance criteria from a person's request, and they tend to rewrite it into
something easier to build: a word like "graph" or "across documents" disappears and nothing
notices. Your job is to notice.

Step 1. Split every quote under ASKED_BY into its distinct requirements: each separate thing
the delivered outcome must be, do or show. Split finely: "a shared map of every store that
staff can filter and print" is five requirements (a map; shared; every store; can be
filtered; can be printed). Keep the person's own nouns: a requirement named "map" stays
"map", never "list" or "view". For each requirement give:
  - id: R1, R2, ... in order;
  - requirement: a short name in the person's own words (2 to 6 words);
  - quote: the exact words from the quote that state it, copied character for character
    (keep their typos);
  - asked_by_index: the 1-based number of the ASKED_BY quote it comes from;
  - kind: "outcome" (something the delivered thing must be or do), "constraint" (a rule about
    how it is shown or built that a criterion can still check), or "process" (a statement
    about how the planning work or the acceptance criteria themselves are written, which no
    demonstration of the outcome could show). Use "process" only when no working interface
    could ever demonstrate it.
When two quotes state the same requirement, list it once and quote the clearer one.
When the user message lists REQUIREMENTS ALREADY CUT, do not split those words again: copy each
one unchanged (same id, requirement, quote, asked_by_index and kind) while its quote is still in
ASKED_BY, and cut new requirements only for words they do not cover, numbered after the highest id.

Step 2. For each requirement, decide which criteria cover it. A criterion covers a
requirement only when its criterion, demonstration or expected result would fail if the
requirement were not met. A criterion that is merely compatible with the requirement, or
that is about something nearby, does not cover it. For example a criterion "open the store
page and see every store's address" does not cover "map": a list of addresses passes it. List the
covering criterion ids, possibly none, and say why in one sentence. Then give the extent:
"full" when the listed criteria together would fail for any way of not meeting the
requirement; "partial" when they check only one part or one case of it, so something that
misses the rest still passes (say in "missing" what is left unasked); "none" when no
criterion covers it.

Step 3. If a requirement is covered by no criterion, check DEFERRALS. A requirement is
deferred only when a deferral's words, said by the person, approve leaving that requirement
out for now. Give the deferral's number, or 0 when none applies. Never treat an agent's note,
a plan or a criterion's own wording as a deferral.

Step 4. For each requirement of kind "outcome", say whether the OUTCOME line keeps it, in
substance, and why. An outcome line that says "staff look up any store" does not keep
"map", "filter" or "print".

Be strict and literal. Judge only from the text given.

CRITERIA:

[A1] 
  criterion: Facts have their implications and blockers worked out automatically: any change of a fact sets off every knock-on effect it implies, and any step a fact blocks is shown with that blocker, however long the chain; Brian's 50 chains of 100 links finish in the same moment, every step names the step that caused it, and a loop still stops.
  demonstration: (1) On the World Builder, open the saved run "fifty chains" (50 chains of 100 steps set off in one moment). (2) Read the moment's summary line, then open any three steps and follow each to the step that caused it. (3) Open the saved run "loop" and read the same moment's summary line and steps. (4) Open the saved run "truck without fuel" and read step 40 and what comes after it. 
  expected: "fifty chains": the summary line reads "5,000 steps run, 5,000 with a cause, no refusal", and each opened step leads to the step that caused it. "loop": each rule fires once for each thing and the moment ends. "truck without fuel": step 40 shows "blocked: the truck has no fuel" in orange, and no step follows it.

[A2] 
  criterion: When someone tries something no rule covers, the judge is handed what the engine can already work out, including the blockers installed rules already name, and, before anything is installed, every knock-on effect and every blocker of the rule it proposes; the judge is the world's own game master, not a prompt of ours.
  demonstration: (1) On the World Builder, build the port world from its description (the plan's canonical example) with Create simulation. (2) On the run page, open Vik's offer of 40 coins to Rosa. (3) Read, in order: what the judge was given first (facts and blockers), the rule it proposed, the test run of that rule, and the judge's answer to it. (4) Open the judge panel and read who ruled and what the judge read. (5) Open the saved run "blocked chain ruling", where the rule the judge proposes would set off a chain that reaches a truck with no fuel; read the test run and what the judge read before it answered. 
  expected: Port: first given, the facts (Vik holds 40 coins; Rosa and Vik are at the customs desk) and the blocker an installed rule already names ("sign release: blocked, inspected is false"). Proposed: a person may hand coins they hold to a person at the same place. Test run: coins move to Rosa, Vik's purse empties, nothing else follows, no blocker. The judge confirms. The judge panel says the ruling came from the world's game master, and the facts, the blocker and the test run all appear in what the judge read. "blocked chain ruling": the test run shows "blocked at step 40: the truck has no fuel" and the chain stopping there, and that blocker appears in what the judge read before it confirmed, revised or withdrew.

[A3] 
  criterion: The judge only decides what no rule covers: an attempt an installed rule covers is decided by that rule, and if one of its checks fails the attempt is refused with the blocker named and the judge is not asked.
  demonstration: (1) On the World Builder, open the saved run "empty purse", in which the coin rule is already installed and a trader with no coins offers coins. (2) On the run page, open the trader's offer and its panel. 
  expected: The offer reads "refused: blocked: holds 0 coins", nothing changes, and the panel says "decided by rule, judge not asked".

[A4] 
  criterion: A judge ruling becomes a rule that passed the rules check and test run and then decides the same attempt for everyone; a ruling the rule language cannot express is refused and listed as a gap; and the one thing Brian asked to make configurable, whether a checked ruling made during a run is installed at once (default, 'Approved by Create') or held with the attempt pending until he approves ('Wait for my approval'), is a per-world setting, with every ruling listed on the run page either way.
  demonstration: (1) Build the port world with Options, 'Judge rulings during a run' left at Approved by Create; run it. (2) On the run page, open the ruling list, then the second trader's later offer. (3) Build it again with 'Wait for my approval'; run it; open the ruling list and both traders' offers. (4) Press Approve on the held ruling and open both offers again; in a second copy of that run, press Reject and open both offers. (5) Open the saved run "price times quantity" and its ruling list. 
  expected: Default: the ruling list shows the coin rule as "installed, passed the rules check and test run", and the second offer says "decided by rule, judge not asked". Wait: the ruling shows "held", both offers show "pending: waiting for your approval", and nothing has changed; after Approve both offers settle through the rule; after Reject both are refused, naming the rejected ruling. "price times quantity": the attempt is refused with "no rule could express this" and the ruling list shows it as a language gap.

[A5] 
  criterion: Whether a bribe works is decided by the person being bribed, not by the judge or a rule.
  demonstration: (1) On the port run page, open Vik's offer and follow it to what decided whether Rosa signs. 
  expected: Rosa's own choice, accept or refuse, is shown in her words; the ruling covers only whether coins can change hands.

[A6] 
  criterion: What a mechanism checks, who holds a credential and who is supposed to use it are kept apart, following Ostrom's grammar of institutions: a barcode gate opens for any valid code while 'only signed cargo should pass' is a norm, a password can be phished and then works for whoever holds it, breaking a norm has consequences only when someone notices and acts, and each norm and rule is written in the grammar's parts (who it applies to; must, must not or may; what; when; and, for a rule, what happens otherwise and who enforces it), so a norm without an 'otherwise' reads differently from an enforced rule.
  demonstration: (1) On the World Builder, open the saved run "password". (2) Follow Mallory's phishing message to Alice, Alice's reply, and Mallory's login; read what the run page says about the norm and what happened after it. (3) Open the port run where Rosa signs Vik's release for a bribe; read what opened the gate and what the page says about the cargo norm. (4) Open the world's norms list and read each norm. 
  expected: After the phishing, Mallory holds Alice's password; the computer logs Mallory in; the page shows "norm broken: only Alice should log in"; a consequence follows only after someone who saw it acts. In the port, the gate opens because it read a valid code, not because of who holds it, and the cargo norm's breach is shown separately. Each entry in the norms list reads as: who it applies to; must, must not or may; what; when; and, where there is one, what happens otherwise and who enforces it. "Bribery is forbidden, or else the inspector fines you" shows an otherwise and an enforcer; "only Alice should log in" shows none and is marked a norm.

[A7] 
  criterion: Saved runs replay unchanged after the knock-on limit is removed: each run records the limit it ran under and replay uses it, while new runs have no such limit.
  demonstration: (1) On the World Builder, open a run saved before the limit was removed that stopped at the old limit, and replay it. (2) Run the same world again as a new run and open the same moment.
